en: One should know that in the Svarāṣṭaka, one word has a single udātta accent, and likewise another has a single svarita; some, however, have two udāttas, while the remainder is traditionally held to be anudātta (unaccented).
In a compound, however, that which has two udātta syllables is seen to have three udātta syllables;
any other such word is traditionally remembered as being entirely anudātta. A svarita following an udātta is called svārya, provided that the two subsequent syllables are not udātta.
That which is thus characterized as having the *svarita* accent should be known as the "natural" (*prākṛta*) one.
(3) If it does not lead to a state of *pracaya* (even when following many *anudātta* syllables), then the *pracaya* preceding both the *svarita* and the *udātta* is suppressed. (4)
When a single [consonant] is prescribed [as following] an acute (udātta) vowel, one should lead that very [consonant] with its own accent;

however, if it occurs at the beginning of a word and is grave (nihata), it may optionally be circumflex (svarita). But after a prescribed acute or even a circumflex vowel, [the subsequent consonant] shall likewise be circumflex.

A *svarita* that follows a *prākṛta* [accent] should be treated as *nihata*; and that which is *aprākṛta* is a *svarita* preceded by a *svara* (acute) or *udātta*. Some teachers, having raised the first half of this [last syllable], pronounce the remainder as a tremulous (*kampita*) *nihata*.

For the *aprākṛta* [svara], they make the first half low and the second high; both the first and second halves are low, while the *svāra* is tremulous in the middle. A Brahmin, being composed, should constantly recite these eight *svaras*.
For he who possesses the darkness-dispelling knowledge of the *svaras* is indeed glorified in the world of Brahman.
